title: Step Pyramid of Djoser: Why It Matters
excerpt: Why the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara matters: built c. 2670 BC by Imhotep as the first monumental stone building. What to see, plus a day tour from Cairo from €33.

Quick answer

The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara matters because it is the world's earliest monumental stone building and Egypt's first pyramid. King Djoser's architect Imhotep raised it around 2670 BC, in the Third Dynasty, and started the pyramid age that ended at Giza. Today you can walk its enclosure wall, colonnade and courtyards, then visit the Imhotep Museum and, on a separate ticket, the Serapeum, all about an hour from central Cairo.

UNESCO describes the pyramid fields from Giza to Dahshur as one World Heritage site.

Most travellers meet Egypt's pyramids at Giza first, so Saqqara, a short drive further south, can sound like an optional detour. It is the opposite. Without the Step Pyramid of Djoser there would be no Great Pyramid to photograph: this is the world's earliest monumental stone building, raised around 2670 BC, and it still shapes how archaeologists read every later Egyptian tomb and temple. This post explains why it changed architecture, what you can actually see at the complex today, and how it fits into a day from Cairo. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure marketplace, lists it on its nine-hour Memphis, Saqqara & Dahshur day, and its team has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

Why the Step Pyramid of Djoser matters

The Step Pyramid of Djoser is important because it is the earliest colossal stone building in Egypt: the first time anywhere that a civilisation raised a monument of this scale in cut stone. Before it, kings were buried under mastabas, flat rectangular tombs of mud brick. Djoser's architect stacked six diminishing tiers to a height of 62.5 metres, creating Egypt's first pyramid and setting the template that Fourth Dynasty kings pushed to perfection at Giza. UNESCO lists the whole pyramid field from Giza to Dahshur, Saqqara included, as World Heritage, inscribed in 1979.

From mud-brick mastaba to pyramid in stages

The pyramid did not begin as a pyramid. The excavator Jean-Philippe Lauer showed that it grew through repeated enlargements, which he labelled M1 to P2: first a square mastaba, then higher and wider additions, and finally six built-up steps. The experiment continued at Meidum and Dahshur, where Sneferu's builders worked out how to make a smooth-sided pyramid. Meidum is on our Fayoum Oasis, Meidum & Hawara day tour, and Dahshur is on the Saqqara day.

Who was Imhotep, the architect behind the Djoser pyramid?

Imhotep was King Djoser's vizier: the official credited with designing the first stone pyramid complex, and one of very few Egyptians of non-royal birth later worshipped as a god. The historian Manetho, writing long afterwards, is usually read as crediting him with the invention of building in hewn stone, and Greek visitors linked him with their healing god Asclepius. Saqqara's site museum is named after him, a rare honour for an architect and a good first stop.

What you see at the Step Pyramid complex today

Today the Djoser complex is much more than one pyramid: a walk through its gateway takes in the enclosure wall, the entrance colonnade, the great courtyard and the South Court, with the pyramid standing at the centre.

  • The pyramid itself. Six stepped tiers, 62.5 m high on a base of about 121 × 109 m. Its polished white limestone casing was stripped away in antiquity.
  • The niched enclosure wall. About 10.5 m high and running over 1.6 km around the complex, with recessed panelling, 14 false doors and one real entrance.
  • The entrance colonnade. A narrow corridor flanked by 40 limestone columns carved to look like bundled reeds.
  • The South Court. Curved boundary stones mark the course of the Heb-sed, the royal jubilee run in which a king proved his fitness to rule.
  • The South Tomb. An underground granite vault far too small for a burial, most likely a symbolic tomb for the king's ka, his life-force. It reopened to visitors after restoration in 2021.

Wear shoes that cope with sand and loose stone. The complex is open, dry and almost treeless, so a hat and water matter from late morning onward.

Can you go inside the Step Pyramid of Djoser?

Sometimes, and you should check on the day. The pyramid's burial chamber, reached by a central shaft, reopened to visitors in March 2020 after a 14-year restoration, but access at Saqqara shifts with conservation work, and when it is open it needs a separate ticket.

What is reliably open is the complex itself, with its enclosure wall, colonnade and courts, on the main Saqqara ticket, which the Sawa day tour includes. If going inside matters to you, ask the guide on your departure.

What else to see at Saqqara: the Imhotep Museum and the Serapeum

Saqqara rewards more time than most itineraries give it. Two stops near the Djoser complex are worth planning around: the Imhotep Museum at the site entrance and the Serapeum, deeper in the necropolis.

The Imhotep Museum, opened in 2006, is named for the pyramid's architect. Its galleries hold statues, reliefs and finds from the Saqqara excavations, a comfortable pause after the enclosure walk. It is covered by the main Saqqara ticket.

The Serapeum is the vast underground gallery where sacred Apis bulls, living manifestations of the god Ptah, were buried in huge granite sarcophagi. It was found in 1851 by the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette. It has its own ticket and is not included on the Sawa day tour.

Visiting the Step Pyramid of Djoser from Cairo: how the day runs

From central Cairo, the Step Pyramid of Djoser is a comfortable day trip, typically about an hour on the road, and combines neatly with Memphis and Dahshur in one departure of about nine hours, with hotel pickup included. The order on the Sawa listing, as of November 2026:

Order Stop
1 Memphis open-air museum: colossal statue of Ramesses II and the alabaster sphinx
2 Saqqara: the Step Pyramid of Djoser complex and enclosure
3 Lunch
4 Dahshur: the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid (the Red Pyramid interior is covered by the site ticket; your guide advises on the day)

The order tells one story. Djoser's successors spent generations learning why a stepped stack could not become a true pyramid; Sneferu cracked the problem at Dahshur, where the Red Pyramid became the first smooth-sided pyramid completed successfully, and his son Khufu took the formula to Giza. For that ending, see the Giza Uncovered half-day tour.

The verdict on the Step Pyramid of Djoser

The Step Pyramid of Djoser is the first chapter of the pyramid story: the earliest monumental stone building on earth, raised for King Djoser around 2670 BC by Imhotep, and still standing at Saqqara. faq.q: How old is the Step Pyramid of Djoser?
faq.a: About 4,700 years. Construction began around 2670 BC, early in the Third Dynasty of Egypt's Old Kingdom, for the king Egyptologists call Djoser, roughly a century before the Great Pyramid of Giza. The pyramid anchors the UNESCO World Heritage property Memphis and its Necropolis, inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979.

faq.q: Why is the Djoser pyramid stepped rather than smooth like Giza's?
faq.a: Because it preserves the experiment, not the answer. The structure grew from stacked mastaba forms translated into stone, enlarged stage by stage into six steps. The smooth-sided pyramid arrived a few reigns later, when King Sneferu perfected the geometry at Dahshur, and Sneferu's son Khufu then applied it at Giza.

faq.q: Is the Step Pyramid of Djoser worth visiting if I am already seeing the Giza pyramids?
faq.a: Yes. It is a different experience, not a repeat. Giza impresses with scale; Djoser shows where scale began, and its enclosure wall, colonnade and courts explain how a whole royal complex worked, not just a tomb. With Memphis and Dahshur added, it makes a full and rewarding pyramid day from Cairo.

faq.q: How far is Saqqara from Cairo?
faq.a: Saqqara sits about 30 km south of Cairo, typically about an hour's drive from central hotels, though traffic can stretch the trip. Public transport is awkward, so most visitors come by tour or private car, which is why Saqqara is usually bundled with Memphis and Dahshur on day itineraries.
